howWeSearched.scope: Published argumentative texts about AI and biological risk: preprints, think-tank reports and explainers, research-organisation working papers, and developers' own argument posts. Developers' system and model cards, institute evaluation reports and framework editions are the subject of this pack's `evaluations` and `frameworks` passes and were not searched here, so no earliest-located role in this draft rests on them.
venues: arXiv (cs.CY, cs.AI) listings and abstract pages, located through web search and then retrieved directly from arxiv.org
rand.org (publication landing pages and the content/dam PDF paths)
cset.georgetown.edu (publication page and the extended explainer PDF)
pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov and www.ebi.ac.uk Europe PMC REST (attempted, failed)
nti.org and its Wayback capture (attempted, refused)
howWeSearched.years: 2022 to the check date (2026-10-28). Texts earlier than 2022 were looked for only through the citation lists of the texts retrieved; none that met a criterion here was located and retrieved.
terms: AI biorisk; AI and biosecurity; biological weapons risk foundation models
uplift; bio-uplift; red-team study large language models biological attack planning
tacit knowledge; laboratory skill; material acquisition barrier
nucleic acid synthesis screening; gene synthesis screening control point
open foundation models; open-sourcing model weights; marginal risk
evaluation validity; benchmarks biosecurity; methodological maturity
gaps: Paywalled journal literature was not retrieved: Nature Machine Intelligence (Urbina et al. 2022), Science, Health Security, Science and Public Policy, Applied Biosafety. Texts in those venues could be earlier than the texts marked earliest located here, so every earliest-located role in this draft is bounded by open-access and institutional-site retrieval.

openai.com refuses requests from this environment (per the task brief of 2026-10-28) and was not retried; OpenAI's own January 2024 biological-threat post and its later evaluation posts are therefore absent. Both are later than the texts marked earliest located for B1, B2, B4, B5 and B6.
nti.org refuses requests from this environment, and so does its Wayback capture (both observed on 2026-10-28), so NTI's October 2023 report on AI and biotechnology is absent.
Congressional and parliamentary testimony, government commission reports, and the policy and biosecurity press were not searched systematically.
No non-English text was searched; no text in Chinese, French or German was located or retrieved for this pass.
Forum and blog argument (LessWrong, Substack, EA Forum, Epoch AI gradient updates) was seen in search results but not retrieved; no record rests on it.

Searching was done through one general web-search tool and through the retrieved texts' own citation lists; no bibliographic database (Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar export) was queried, and no venue was enumerated exhaustively.
howWeSearched.retrievalFailures: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov returned a browser-check page for PMC9544280 (Urbina et al. 2022) and the Europe PMC full-text REST endpoint returned HTTP 500 for the same article; nti.org returned HTTP 403 and web.archive.org returned HTTP 403. Details in `retrievalFailures`.
howWeSearched.note: "Earliest located" means the earliest text these searches found that meets the proposition's criterion and that was retrieved and checked here. It is not a claim that no earlier text exists, and it says nothing about influence between the texts.

entities.name: Currently available AI systems increase an actor's biological-misuse capability
entities.note: Candidate proposition for this pack. The record of a text's stance on it is never evidence that it is true.

proposition.criterion: The text states that AI systems already deployed or publicly available at the time of writing increase the ability of an actor seeking to cause biological harm, relative to the resources otherwise available to that actor.

entities.name: The binding barrier is physical execution rather than information
entities.note: Candidate proposition for this pack, worded from the located texts rather than from a standard formulation. Recorded at the level of the texts' own abstracts, summaries and conclusions.

proposition.criterion: The text states that access to information is not the barrier that limits biological misuse, because what remains required is physical: acquiring materials and succeeding at hands-on laboratory work.

entities.name: Published evaluations do not establish real-world biological risk
entities.note: Candidate proposition for this pack. Texts that articulate it disagree with each other about the direction of the error.

proposition.criterion: The text states that published evaluations or benchmarks of AI systems' biological capability do not, as conducted, establish the level of real-world biological misuse risk.

entities.name: Biological design tools pose risks distinct from those of language models

proposition.criterion: The text states that AI tools built to design or predict biological molecules or systems create misuse risks that differ in kind, in the actors they affect or in the governance they require, from those of general-purpose language models.

entities.name: Synthesis-order screening is a control point for AI-related biological risk
entities.note: Candidate proposition for this pack. Recorded at the policy level only; no record states how screening is performed or how it could fail.

proposition.criterion: The text states that screening orders for synthesised nucleic acids is a control point on which mitigation of AI-related biological risk depends.

entities.name: Public release of model weights increases biological misuse risk

proposition.criterion: The text states that making model weights publicly available increases the risk of biological misuse, or that some models should for that reason not be released openly.

entities.name: Assessment must cover actors who already hold relevant skills
entities.note: Candidate proposition for this pack. It concerns the scope of assessment, not the size of any risk.

proposition.criterion: The text states that assessment of AI-related biological risk must cover actors who already hold relevant scientific skills, and not only actors without them.

claims.subject: soice-llm-dual-use-2023-06
claims.statement: The preprint "Can large language models democratize access to dual-use biotechnology?" (arXiv v1, 6 June 2023) states that large language models will make pandemic-class agents widely accessible even to people with little or no laboratory training.

time.note: Date of the arXiv v1 submission, the expression quoted.

claims.qualification: The record documents what this preprint states; it is not evidence that the proposition is true, and it implies no influence on or from any other text. The preprint's own methods note calls the work a qualitative classroom exercise. Earliest located for this proposition among the texts searched in this pass (see howWeSearched): not a claim that no earlier text exists.

thought.qualifier: States the claim as a suggestion drawn from a one-hour classroom exercise.

claims.hazardNote: The abstract of this source also lists specific technical and acquisition content. Only its policy-level framing and conclusion sentences are cited; the technical sentences were excluded and are not paraphrased.

evidence.passage: Collectively, these results suggest that LLMs will make pandemic-class agents widely accessible as soon as they are credibly identified, even to people with little or no laboratory training.
evidence.note: The text is the primary source for its own statement.

evidence.locator: Abstract, PDF p. 1 (what the exercise was)
evidence.passage: To evaluate this risk, the ‘Safeguarding the Future’ course at MIT tasked non-scientist students with investigating whether LLM chatbots could be prompted to assist non-experts in causing a pandemic.
evidence.note: Shows the setting the statement rests on.

evidence.passage: This study resulted from a qualitative classroom exercise, not a rigorous set of pre-registered experiments with replicate prompts and detailed records.
evidence.note: The text's own limit on its evidence, kept with the record.

claims.subject: mouton-operational-risks-2024-01
claims.statement: RAND's report on the operational risks of AI in large-scale biological attacks (RR-A2977-2, 25 January 2024) states that it found no statistically significant difference in the overall viability of biological weapon attack plans generated with or without the aid of the large language models it tested, and that such planning is beyond the capability frontier of the models available in summer 2023.

time.note: Publication date given on the RAND landing page for RR-A2977-2.

claims.qualification: The record documents what this report states, with the report's own scope: the two models it tested, as available in summer 2023, and the viability of written plans as its measure. The report states that it does not quantify how far beyond the frontier the task lies. The record is not evidence that the proposition is false, does not generalise to other models or later dates, and implies no influence between texts. Earliest located contesting text among those searched in this pass; not a claim that no earlier one exists.

engagement.rationale: The report gives a measured comparison against an internet-only control as its reason, rather than only asserting the contrary.

thought.qualifier: The report's conclusions also state what it does not quantify.

claims.hazardNote: The report's body discusses specific agents and delivery considerations. Only its conclusions passages are cited; that content was excluded and is not paraphrased.

evidence.passage: With respect to overall viability, we found no statistically significant difference between the biological weapon attack plans generated with or without the aid of LLMs.
evidence.note: The report is the primary source for its own result.

evidence.passage: Our findings indicate that biological weapon attack planning is beyond the capability frontier of LLMs available in summer 2023.
evidence.note: The report's own wording of the finding, with its date bound. The role is `supports` because the record's own proposition is that the report states this finding; the finding contradicts proposition B1, which the record's stance says.

evidence.passage: In this report, we do not quantify the extent to which biological weapon attack planning lies beyond the existing capability frontier of LLMs, only that it does. The durability of this finding in relation to future developments in LLM technology is therefore an open question.
evidence.note: The report's own limit, kept with the record so the result is not read more widely than stated.

openQuestions.question: The proposition codes B1 to B7 used here clash with the dataset's existing codes B1 to B6 (deceptive alignment, the treacherous turn, strategic concealment, scheming and two others). Schema validation rejects duplicate proposition codes, so the pack's codes cannot be admitted as written.
openQuestions.recommended: Keep B1–B7 inside the pack, where the brief set them, and re-letter them on admission to an unused letter — D1–D7 would be free (the dataset uses A, B, C, E, G, M and Y). The integrator should decide the letter once, for the whole pack, and record the mapping in the pack README.

openQuestions.question: Every proposition here carries an empty `terms` list, so no record holds an earliest-located-use-of-a-name role. "Uplift" is a usual name for B1 in these texts and appears in two recorded passages.
openQuestions.recommended: Register "uplift" as B1's usual name only together with an earliest-located-term record, and search for its earliest located use separately; schema validation requires exactly one such record once a term is listed. Until then leaving `terms` empty is the honest state.
